The father knew his daughter was already safe with the police—not held by the kidnapper—so the smartphone ransom demand was false and paying it would be pointless. His knowledge that she was in police custody meant the “kidnapping” could not be real, and that is why he decided the one hundred million yen ransom should not be paid.

The father refused to pay because he believed paying the one hundred million yen would not save his daughter: the kidnappers were likely to kill her once they received the money, so handing over the ransom was a trap rather than a rescue. He therefore decided not to pay. The call itself and the kidnappers’ demand did not make him think the kidnapping was fake; rather, his fear that the daughter would be killed regardless—and that delivering the money would make the situation worse—was the reason for his refusal.

The father believed the kidnapper intended to kill the hostage—and possibly him—at the handover, so paying the ransom would mean walking into a trap rather than saving his daughter. Although he initially did not think the kidnapping itself was fake, his belief that the kidnappers would not honor a release after receiving the money made him decide not to pay. The essential reason was that compliance would put his daughter and himself in greater danger, not that the demand was simply a hoax.

The father decided not to pay the one hundred million yen because he believed the kidnappers would kill his daughter once they got the money, and that the handover was a trap that would put them in greater danger. Although he did not think the kidnapping was fake, he concluded that complying would not save her—so refusing to pay was his only chance of protecting her.
